avoid.reason: Pickpocketing on tram 28, in Baixa/Alfama and the metro; persistent (fake) drug hawkers in the centre

hood_desc: Alfama is Lisbon's oldest quarter, a maze of steep cobbled alleys, fado houses and viewpoints beneath the castle, ideal for travelers wanting historic charm and atmosphere.
Bairro Alto is the city's bohemian nightlife hub, quiet by day and packed with bars, restaurants and music by night, perfect for partygoers and night owls.
Chiado is the elegant, cultured shopping district of historic cafes, theaters and boutiques between Bairro Alto and Baixa, suited to stylish and first-time visitors.
Baixa is the flat, grand downtown grid of pedestrian streets, plazas and shops rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake, a central, convenient base for sightseers.
Belém is the riverside monumental district of the Jerónimos Monastery, Belém Tower and famous custard tarts, great for families and history and culture lovers.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though many locals prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: You can now tap a contactless bank card or phone directly at Metro gates and on Carris buses and trams. Otherwise buy a navegante occasional card (0.50 EUR) from metro station machines and load singles (about 1.85 EUR) or the 24-hour pass (~7 EUR/~US$8) covering metro, buses, trams and funiculars. Buying on board tram 28 costs much more, so tap or pre-load instead.
transit.hours: The Metro runs 6:30am-1am daily; after that Carris night buses ('rede da madrugada') take over.

transit.m: Metro Red Line from Aeroporto toward the center (25 min)
Carris bus 744 or 783 to central Lisbon (35 min)

landmarks: Belém Tower
A UNESCO-listed 16th-century fortified tower on the Tagus riverfront, its Manueline stonework makes it Lisbon's most photographed monument.
Jerónimos Monastery
An ornate UNESCO World Heritage monastery in Belém whose limestone cloisters are a masterpiece of Manueline architecture.
Praça do Comércio
A grand riverside square framed by yellow arcaded buildings and a triumphal arch, offering classic wide shots of the Tagus.
São Jorge Castle
A hilltop Moorish castle overlooking the city, prized for panoramic sunset views over Lisbon's terracotta rooftops.
Elevador da Glória
A charming yellow funicular climbing a steep, tile-lined street, one of the most Instagrammed corners of the city.
Águas Livres Aqueduct
An 18th-century stone aqueduct with dramatic pointed arches spanning the Alcântara valley, striking for architecture photography.
Lisbon Cathedral (Sé de Lisboa)
The city's fortress-like Romanesque cathedral, dating to 1147, framed beautifully by passing yellow trams.
Cristo Rei (Christ the King)
A towering hilltop statue across the river modeled on Rio's Christ the Redeemer, offering sweeping views of Lisbon.
25 de Abril Bridge
A massive red suspension bridge reminiscent of San Francisco's Golden Gate, iconic in skyline and river shots.
National Pantheon (Church of Santa Engrácia)
A grand domed baroque church on the Lisbon skyline, its white cupola is a distinctive landmark for cityscape photos.

train.note: There are currently no direct international trains from Lisbon: the Sud Expresso and Lusitania sleepers to Spain were withdrawn in 2020 and have not returned. Reaching Madrid by rail means a slow 3-train combo via Entroncamento and Badajoz; Portugal's only cross-border train is the Porto-Vigo Celta. Most people take the coach or fly.

bus.note: Direct coaches to Spain (including overnight departures) leave mainly from Oriente and Sete Rios terminals and take ~8h to Madrid. Rede Expressos (rede-expressos.pt) covers domestic routes.

ferry.note: Lisbon has no international passenger ferries - only cruise calls. The orange Tagus river ferries (Transtejo) to Cacilhas and Barreiro are handy local crossings with great views.
